html:
A Greek physician from the island of Kos, born around 460 BCE, called the father of medicine. Little is known for sure about his life; Plato mentions him as a famous doctor who taught for a fee.

About sixty medical texts, the Hippocratic Corpus, carry his name, but they were written by many authors over a long period. Their key idea is that illness has natural causes, not divine ones. The treatise On the Sacred Disease argues that epilepsy is no more sacred than any other disease. The texts urge doctors to observe patients closely, record cases, and pay attention to diet, climate and environment. Some explain health as a balance of four humours, a theory that Galen later built on and that ruled Western medicine until the 1800s.

The Hippocratic Oath, a promise of medical ethics, is part of the collection. His followers worked in the same age as the healing sanctuaries of Asclepius, which offered a religious path to cure.
